summary: Background: Head circumference (HC) is a routine clinical parameter in pediatric patients indicating brain growth and neurodevelopment. Although usually obtained with a tape measure, this method is operator-dependent and prone to variability. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides a retrospective alternative, but existing imaging-based approaches can be limited by predefined measurement planes, restricted clinician review, and cranial surface artifacts. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate a clinician-guided software tool for measuring pediatric HC from routinely acquired 3D MRI examinations. Methods: We developed a desktop application in Python using PySide6, the Insight Segmentation and Registration Toolkit, and the Visualization Toolkit for MRI-based HC measurement. The workflow included outer skin surface reconstruction, placement of 3 landmarks to define a freely orientable measurement plane, contour extraction, and circumference calculation. Optional Delaunay-based interpolation was implemented to reduce the influence of local cranial surface irregularities. In this retrospective evaluation, the tool was applied to 23 pediatric MRI examinations, including 18 without and 5 with clinically identified cranial surface irregularities. Two clinicians independently performed 3 repeated software measurements per examination. Median software measurements were compared with a single tape-based HC measurement obtained on the date of MRI. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman analysis, mean absolute error (MAE), proportional bias analysis, and a linear mixed-effects model. Interrater differences and preliminary usability feedback were also evaluated. Results: Software-based HC measurement was feasible in all 23 examinations. In cases without cranial surface irregularities, the raw and interpolated contours showed similar agreement with tape-based measurements (bias 0.415 cm and 0.410 cm; MAE 0.429 cm and 0.423 cm, respectively). In the 5 examinations with irregularities, the intersection contour showed a greater bias of 1.420 cm and wider limits of agreement (LoA; −0.182 to 3.021 cm), whereas the interpolated contour showed a lower bias of 0.448 cm and narrower LoA (−0.119 to 1.014 cm). The estimated coefficient for the contour-by-subgroup interaction was −0.967 cm (SE 0.195 cm, 95% CI −1.349 to −0.584 cm; <.001). No statistically significant proportional trend was detected, although the analysis had limited power to exclude proportional bias. Interrater differences were small. The 2 clinicians reported System Usability Scale scores of 92.5 and 95.0, representing preliminary descriptive feedback. Conclusions: The clinician-guided workflow enabled MRI-based HC measurement in all examined cases and showed small interrater differences. Delaunay-based interpolation was associated with closer agreement with tape-based measurements in the small subgroup with cranial surface irregularities, while both contour variants performed similarly in examinations without irregularities. These findings are preliminary because of the small cohort, the single tape-based reference measurement per patient, and the 5-case irregularity subgroup. Larger studies using repeated reference measurements and broader cranial morphologies are needed to validate the workflow.
title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging–Based Measurement of Pediatric Head Circumference by a Clinician-in-the-Loop 3D Surface Tool: Development and Validation Study

summary: Background: Serum urate testing requires venipuncture; urine dipstick testing is inexpensive and routine. Whether dipstick results add information on hyperuricemia beyond age, sex, and BMI is unknown. Objective: This study aims to develop and externally validate machine learning models estimating the probability of hyperuricemia from 9 dipstick fields, age, sex, and BMI, and to quantify what the dipstick adds. Methods: The development dataset included 129,535 adults with first urine tests and same-day serum urate and BMI measurements at a Korean tertiary hospital (2010-2025); 21,124 had urate levels ≥7.0 mg/dL, and 81.6% (n=105,704) had a same-day health checkup. Calibrated 12-input ensembles of Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Categorical Boosting (CatBoost) were trained on a person-level 80% split (103,628 persons) for serum urate ≥7.0 mg/dL (primary) and ≥9.0 mg/dL (secondary). They were tested in the remaining 25,907 persons (4225 events at ≥7.0 mg/dL) and in 49,987 adults in the KNHANES (Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey; 2016-2024; 5068 events). Inputs, KNHANES coding, split, and training procedure were fixed before fitting. We assessed discrimination, calibration, operating points by sex, decision curves, and increments over age-sex-BMI models. Results: At ≥7.0 mg/dL, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.825 (95% CI 0.820-0.831) internally and 0.845 (95% CI 0.840-0.849) externally, but 0.710 in men and 0.795 in women. Across 4 model classes, the dipstick added 0.017 to 0.024 to the external AUROC of age-sex-BMI models (0.814-0.823), or 3.1 cases per 1000 screened with top-10% referral. Externally, the models overpredicted (observed-to-expected ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.71-0.75); an intercept update fitted in half of KNHANES restored it to 1.00 in the other half. The internally derived 80%-sensitivity threshold flagged 29.8% (14,916/49,987) of adults, 97.4% (14,533/14,916) of them men; sensitivity was 77.1% (3907/5068) overall but 10.1% (53/527) in women, and positive predictive value (PPV) was 26.2% (3907/14,916). Flagging all men gave 89.6% (4541/5068) sensitivity and slightly less net benefit than the model at threshold probabilities up to 10%. At ≥9.0 mg/dL, external results were AUROC 0.860, increment 0.052 to 0.074 (1.6 cases per 1000), observed-to-expected ratio 0.48, scaled Brier score 0.002 (no better than predicting the prevalence), and PPV 2.6% at 82% sensitivity. Conclusions: Routine dipstick results add a small increment to age, sex, and BMI for identifying serum urate ≥7.0 mg/dL. Ranking transferred from the hospital to a national survey sample, but absolute risk did not, and at the tested thresholds the models mainly selected men. Both cohorts comprised people who had blood drawn, so triage of serum urate testing in urine-only encounters, in which BMI is usually missing, remains an untested hypothesis. Before any use, the models would need local recalibration and evaluation in the intended setting.
title: Machine Learning Models Combining Routine Urine Dipstick Results With Age, Sex, and BMI to Triage Serum Urate Testing: Development and External Validation Study

summary: Background: The growing demand for pathology services and the shortage of pathologists in China have created an urgent need for innovative tools to improve diagnostic efficiency and support professional practice. Large language models (LLMs) may assist pathologists in clinical practice, scientific research, and medical education, but their implementation depends on many factors, such as pathologists’ awareness and willingness to adopt these technologies. Objective: This study aimed to assess Chinese pathologists’ awareness, practical experience, perceptions, ethical concerns regarding LLMs; their willingness to adopt LLMs; and factors associated with willingness to use LLMs in pathology. Methods: A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted among certified pathologists practicing in mainland China. The survey assessed participants’ demographic and professional characteristics; LLM awareness, use, and perceived performance in clinical practice, scientific research, and medical education; ethical concerns; and suggestions for future improvement. Questionnaire reliability and validity were assessed using Cronbach α, Guttman Lambda 6, and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure. Group differences in perceived performance were examined using Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment. Factors associated with willingness to use LLMs in pathology were measured as the summed score of three 5-point Likert items and analyzed using ordinal logistic regression. Results: Of 339 eligible pathologists, 248 (73.2%) had heard of LLMs, and 64 of these (25.8%) had used them. ChatGPT was the most recognized and most commonly used model. Compared with nonusers, LLM users rated clinical applications more cautiously, particularly for analyzing patient data, organizing medical history, and supporting the understanding of disease mechanisms and treatments; these differences were significant after domain-specific FDR adjustment (adjusted P=.02) but borderline after overall correction across all performance items (adjusted P=.05). Perceptions of research and educational applications did not differ significantly between users and nonusers. A higher education level, attending physicians (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.39, 95% CI 1.09-5.22; P=.029), chief physicians (aOR 4.64, 95% CI 1.57-13.69; P=.005), and more than 43 weekly working hours (aOR 2.33, 95% CI 1.40-3.89; P=.001) were associated with greater willingness to use LLMs, whereas working in fourth- or lower-tier cities (aOR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22-0.79; P=.007) and reading 1001-3000 slides annually (aOR 0.43, 95% CI 0.20-0.94; P=.034) were associated with less willingness. Major ethical concerns included model transparency, sensitive data security, and academic misuse. Conclusions: Chinese pathologists show high awareness of LLMs and generally favorable attitudes toward their potential application in pathology, but actual use is limited. The gap between awareness and use highlights the need for improved accessibility, targeted training, pathology-specific validation, workflow integration, and ethical governance. Future implementation should emphasize locally adapted models, data security, and equitable access, particularly for pathologists in lower-tier cities and resource-limited settings.
title: Chinese Pathologists’ Adoption of Large Language Models: Cross-Sectional Survey on Influencing Factors

summary: Background: Few studies have investigated automated case finding in hospital-based cancer registries despite their crucial role in supporting population-based surveillance. In these settings, data completeness is often compromised by referral patterns, yet the influence of weakly supervised learning strategies on model performance remains underexplored. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different supervision approaches (inaccurate, inexact, and report-level labeling) on deep learning model performance for cancer case finding in a hospital-based registry setting and assess model generalizability across patient-level and report-level classification tasks. Methods: Hospital-based cancer registry and pathology report data from Songklanagarind Hospital (2005-2023) were used for model development and evaluation. Three labeling approaches were implemented: inaccurate (all reports from patients with cancer labeled positive), inexact (concatenated reports from patients with cancer labeled positive), and report-level (only registrar-annotated tumor-related reports labeled positive). Model performance was evaluated on max-pooled, concatenated, and individual report classification tasks using a simple word embedding model, multilayer perceptron, recurrent neural network, convolutional neural network (CNN), and hierarchical self-attention network architectures. Results: Models trained using weakly supervised labeling achieved the highest performance across patient-level evaluation tasks, and CNN models consistently showed superior performance. While report-level labeling yielded superior accuracy for individual reports, it suffered substantial degradation in patient-level evaluations. This suggests that models trained on curated data overfitted to primary tumor patterns, failing to recognize secondary evidence (eg, metastatic or surveillance findings). Conversely, weakly supervised approaches enabled the detection of patients with cancer via diverse report types. Error analysis revealed that false negatives were primarily driven by insufficient institutional data—specifically, referred patients lacking primary diagnostic reports—rather than algorithmic failure. Conclusions: In this single tertiary referral hospital setting, weakly supervised labeling outperformed report-level human annotation for patient-level case finding, whereas report-level labeling performed best for individual report classification. The CNN architecture achieved the highest or near-highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve in most configurations.
title: Development and Application of Deep Learning Models for Case Finding From Pathology Reports in a Hospital-Based Cancer Registry: Algorithm Development and Validation

summary: Background: Under the new diagnosis-related group (NDRG) payment system in Korea, the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (HIRA) applies disease-specific diagnosis coding approval criteria that differ from the coding guidelines of the Korean Classification of Diseases (KCD), frequently leading to claim denials for conditions such as acute kidney injury, pleural effusion, and malnutrition. Repeated denials also induce conservative down-coding among coders. Because denial notifications are issued 9 to 18 months after discharge, reactive, denial-triggered quality management is insufficient. Objective: We implemented a metadata-driven rule repository that operationalizes HIRA’s review criteria as data, coupled with a daily-refreshed screening data mart (encompassing 6 clinical data domains and 14 data sources) and a robotic process automation (RPA) notification pipeline, to enable proactive, preclaim coding quality management. Methods: This Implementation Report describes the design, deployment, and 12-month operational experience of the system at an 820-bed NDRG pilot hospital. HIRA’s criteria were externalized into a 4-layer rule repository—criteria definitions, clinical concepts, disease-specific attributes, and decision rules. A nightly extract, transform, and load pipeline populates a patient-by-attribute screening data mart within the clinical data warehouse; each morning, Python-based RPA compiles and emails review candidate lists to coders. Descriptive statistics summarized coverage and detection outcomes; precision (equivalent to positive predictive value) was calculated with Wilson score 95% CIs. Implementation (Results): At the end of the evaluation period, the rule repository comprised 11 review criteria, 271 clinical concepts, 77 attributes, and 96 decision rules. Over the 12-month evaluation period (July 2025 to June 2026), the system evaluated 17,138 diagnosis- or episode-level targets across 15,388 distinct episodes—67% of the hospital’s 22,970 NDRG episodes—and flagged 576 (3.4%) review candidates, of which 50 (8.7%, 95% CI 6.6%-11.3%) were confirmed by coders as actual coding errors. The proportion of confirmed coding errors among review candidates differed significantly across the 3 monitored categories (=39.9; <.001): present-on-admission (POA) coding items showed the highest precision (20/82, 24%), followed by the NDRG cost-outlier category (17/134, 12.7%) and frequently denied diagnoses (13/360, 3.6%). The system was designed, built, and operated by existing departmental staff without additional budget or dedicated IT support, required an estimated 1 to 1.5 hours of coder review time per week, and has continued to operate daily on weekdays since launch. Conclusions: A metadata-driven rule repository integrated with a daily screening data mart and RPA can operationalize payer review criteria as versioned data rather than hard-coded logic, enabling proactive coding surveillance before claim submission. The approach was implemented without additional budget or dedicated IT staff, but its performance may vary across institutions. Further validation against formal HIRA review outcomes and multi-institutional evaluation are needed to establish its performance and transferability across NDRG hospitals.
title: Development and Evaluation of a Metadata-Driven Rule Repository and Daily Screening System for Diagnosis Coding Compliance Under the Korean New Diagnosis-Related Group Payment System: Implementation Report

summary: Background: The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) is a standard instrument for risk adjustment in the secondary use of clinical data. Its coding algorithms require ( codes with at least 4 characters. Hospital data integration centers may truncate codes to 3 characters for privacy. Truncation makes subcodes ambiguous across Charlson groups and can render the CCI noncomputable. Objective: The primary objective was to develop, openly release, and evaluate computational strategies that estimate the CCI from 3-character codes using national 4-character subcode frequencies from the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis). The secondary objective was to identify and quantify potential error caused by truncation and error induced by the national prior. Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study analyzed 507,949 inpatient encounters of 243,677 patients from University Hospital Mannheim (UMM; 2010‐2024). The open-source R (The R Foundation) package (version 1.0.0; developed by Gaetan Kamdje Wabo et al.) implements a deterministic interval estimator (S1), an exact expected-value estimator (S2), multiple imputation (S3), a Dirichlet-smoothed predictive median (S4), and a cross-validated Meta Learner. Age-conditioned priors came from Destatis table 23131‐01. The reference standard was the Quan-weighted CCI computed from full-length codes. We report mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), Bland-Altman limits, Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) distance, and exact agreement with patient-level cluster bootstrap 95% CIs. Robustness analyses covered hyperparameters, a local oracle prior, prefixes without Destatis subcodes, Bonferroni-corrected subgroups, and nested cross-validation. Results: S2, S3, and S4 achieved nearly identical MAE. S2 reached 0.1394 (95% CI 0.1379‐0.1408), S3 reached 0.1395 (95% CI 0.1380‐0.1408), and S4 reached 0.1390 (95% CI 0.1374‐0.1405). All 3 were more accurate than S1 (MAE 0.1678, 95% CI 0.1660-0.1695) and the Meta Learner (MAE 0.1451, 95% CI 0.1437-0.1465). S2 computes exactly the expected score that S3 approximates by sampling, which explains their near-identical errors. S4 preserved the reference distribution best (KS distance 0.023, exact agreement 87.0%). The Meta Learner attained the lowest squared error (RMSE 0.318), also under nested cross-validation. In paired testing within a random subsample of 10,000 patients, S4 at its default setting did not differ from the best S3 setting. Under an in-sample oracle prior, 73% to 90% of the MAE of S2 to S4 remained, and prior mismatch accounted for the rest. After Bonferroni correction, 10 of 20 chapters retained a decisive best strategy. Conclusions: In this single-center cohort, frequency-informed estimation reconstructed the CCI from 3-character codes with an MAE of about 0.14 points (S2: 0.1394, 95% CI 0.1379-0.1408; S3: 0.1395, 95% CI 0.1380-0.1408; S4: 0.1390, 95% CI 0.1374-0.1405). Expected-value estimation (S2) is the most parsimonious choice for encounter-level accuracy. The integer-valued median (S4) can suit analyses that depend on the score distribution. Use in clinical research remains a potential application that requires multisite validation.
title: Estimating the Charlson Comorbidity Index From Privacy-Truncated Diagnosis Codes: Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study Evaluating Five Computational Strategies in 507,949 Inpatient Encounters

summary: Background: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is one of the major causes of preventable blindness in premature infants. Early screening, accurate diagnosis, and severity classification are crucial for reducing irreversible visual impairment. Recently, image-based AI models have been widely applied to ROP screening, diagnosis, and severity classification. However, the model architecture, data source, validation method, and diagnostic task vary across studies. Consequently, the overall diagnostic efficiency and clinical utility of deep learning (DL) remain to be systematically assessed. Objective: This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of image-based AI for ROP by disease type, validation method, model type, and use of transfer learning (TL). Methods: We performed a systematic search across Web of Science, Embase, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, and Cochrane Library as of October 12, 2026, to identify studies investigating image-based AI for ROP detection or clinical subtype classification. The risk of bias (RoB) of included studies was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled using bivariate mixed-effects models, with analyses stratified by diagnostic task and validation method. Results: Sixty-two studies contributed 185 contingency tables. For normal vs ROP, pooled sensitivity was 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.96) and specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.94-0.97). For normal vs treatment-requiring ROP (TR-ROP), sensitivity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.91-0.99) and specificity was 0.74 (95% CI 0.66-0.80). For mild vs severe ROP, specificity was 0.78 (95% CI 0.59-0.90). In external validation, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.95 (95% CI 0.89-0.97) and 0.83 (95% CI 0.72-0.90), respectively, while the corresponding estimates were 0.95 (95% CI 0.93-0.96) and 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) in internal validation. For DL and conventional machine learning (ML) models, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98), respectively, while specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.95-0.97) and 0.91 (95% CI 0.84-0.94), respectively. With and without TL, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.95 (95% CI 0.92-0.97), respectively, while specificity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) and 0.92 (95% CI 0.86-0.95), respectively. Conclusions: Image-based AI may have high sensitivity for ROP assessment, but its specificity is lower for identifying TR-ROP and in the external-validation subgroup. Given the predominance of retrospective studies, heterogeneity, and limited external validation, current evidence supports AI as an adjunct to screening and referral, with clinicians retaining responsibility for diagnostic and treatment decisions. Prospective, multicenter external validation is needed. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261418502; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261418502
title: Image-Based AI for the Diagnosis of Retinopathy of Prematurity: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: Background: Clinical decision-making is inherently shaped by contextual factors that extend beyond guideline-based knowledge and objective clinical parameters. Although clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) aim to improve decision quality and safety, many existing systems insufficiently account for such contextual influences, limiting their effectiveness and acceptance. A prerequisite for a context-sensitive CDSS is the systematic and standardized representation of context factors. However, the extent to which existing clinical terminologies are capable of representing these factors remains unclear. Objective: This study investigates the terminological representability of empirically identified context factors that influence clinical decision-making using SNOMED CT (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine—Clinical Terms) as the semantic interoperability standard. Methods: The analysis builds on a previously established set of context concepts identified through a scoping review of empirical literature and organized within a hierarchical conceptual structure. An exploratory manual semantic mapping of these context concepts to SNOMED CT was conducted. Mapping quality was assessed using standardized equivalence classifications (equal, equivalent, wider, narrower, inexact, and unmatched). An independent expert review and consensus process ensured harmonized mapping results. Context concepts not represented in SNOMED CT were also examined using alternative vocabularies via the OHDSI (Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics) Athena platform. Results: In total, 189 context concepts were analyzed. Of these, 81.5% (n=154) could be mapped to existing SNOMED CT concepts. Semantic correspondence varied across the analyzed context concepts: 36% (n=68) were classified as equal, 21.2% (n=40) as equivalent, 8.5% (n=16) as wider, 13.8% (n=26) as narrower, and 2.1% (n=4) as inexact. The remaining 18.5% (n=35) were classified as unmatched, indicating that no suitable SNOMED CT correspondence was identified. Patient-related context concepts demonstrated the highest coverage (70/75, 93.3%), whereas institution-related concepts showed substantially lower coverage (7/14, 50%). Mapped concepts were distributed across 11 SNOMED CT domains, most frequently observable entity and qualifier value. Entity-specific analyses revealed differences in both terminological coverage and equivalence status. A majority of nonrepresented concepts were identified in alternative vocabularies, primarily MeSH (23/35, 65.7%) and LOINC (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes; 10/35, 28.6%), albeit often with inexact or partial correspondence. Conclusions: The findings indicate that a substantial proportion of empirically identified context factors influencing clinical decision-making can be terminologically represented in SNOMED CT, although relevant gaps persist, particularly for organizational and social context factors. These results highlight both the potential and the limitations of existing clinical terminologies for supporting context-sensitive CDSSs and provide a foundation for future work on semantic standardization, ontology development, and the integration of standardized contextual information into CDSSs.
title: Assessing the Terminological Representation of Context Factors in Clinical Decision-Making Using SNOMED CT: Exploratory Analysis Study

summary: Background: Successful digital health initiatives require a sustainable health informatics (HI) workforce. The lack of standardized job roles across health sectors may result in fragmented HI workforce planning. Objective: This study aimed to develop a framework to guide HI workforce planning in Saudi Arabia aligned with two strategic branches of the Health Sector Transformation Program (HSTP): (1) governance and regulation and (2) data and digitalization. Methods: A 4-phase qualitative exploratory study was conducted. In phase 1, semistructured interviews were conducted with Saudi HI experts identified through purposive sampling based on preset inclusion criteria: (1) a master’s degree or higher in HI or a related field; (2) at least 10 years of experience; and (3) a current leadership, planning, or management role in digital health. Of the experts approached, 17 agreed to participate. Saturation was confirmed retrospectively. Content analysis was used to identify HI job roles necessary to achieve the HSTP. Phase 2 involved 3 researchers mapping the identified job roles to the relevant HSTP branch and to the 4 strategic objectives under data and digitalization. In phase 3, a health-related sector guide was developed based on reviewing nationally published documents. In phase 4, HI job roles were mapped to 3 job levels and to the health sectors. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participant demographics and the distribution of job roles across job levels, HSTP branches and objectives, and health sectors. Results: The sample had a nearly balanced gender distribution; 88.2% (15/17) held a master’s degree and most (6/17, 35.3%) had 10 to 15 years of experience. Interviews identified 62 HI job roles relevant to the HSTP, of which 21 (33.9%) were mapped to the strategic objective of unified electronic health records for all under the branch of data and digitalization and 19 (30.6%) were mapped to the health sector governance and regulation branch. A health-related sector guide identified 6 potential employment sectors: health care provider organizations, health care authorities and agencies, health IT companies, research institutions, academic institutions, and health insurance. Job roles were further mapped to job levels and sectors: middle-level roles were most common (24/62, 38.7%), followed by entry-level (21/62, 33.9%) and top-level (17/62, 27.4%) roles. Health care provider organizations (55/62, 88.7%) and health care authorities and agencies (49/62, 79%) accounted for the largest share of sectors. The most frequently identified roles were health business analyst, chief information officer, HI specialist, data analyst, HI manager, and health care data scientist. Conclusions: Findings identified job paths for HI professionals as identified by experts. These results may guide workforce planning and curriculum development. By clarifying roles and optimizing workforce placement, these findings help identify unique and overlapping positions between HI and other health specialists to ensure efficient use of human capital.
title: Aligning Health Informatics Workforce Roles With Saudi Arabia’s Health Sector Transformation Program: Multiphase Qualitative Study

summary: Background: The geriatric 4Ms framework conceptualizes 4 evidence-based elements (ie, Mobility, Mentation, Medication, and what Matters) that are important to high-quality care for older adults. Improving on these measures is central to the Age-Friendly Health Systems initiative. Electronic health records (EHRs) are critical to modern health systems including being able to review patient information and act on geriatric health concerns. Objective: This study aimed to examine how clinicians use a commercial EHR to access 4Ms-relevant information during inpatient and emergency care of older adults to inform the design of scalable, age-friendly 4Ms EHR tools. Methods: We interviewed clinicians and clinical staff (n=20), including physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses, pharmacists, and physical therapists from 5 large academic health systems across the United States regarding their experiences using the EHR during inpatient and emergency care for older adults. All included health systems used the same EHR and had geriatric quality programs in place. Participants completed virtual interviews that included narrated walkthroughs of their local EHR builds in response to 3 brief clinical vignettes focused on falls, home care needs, and delirium. Interviews were screen-recorded with audio and transcribed for coding and thematic analysis. Results: Major themes spanned the 4Ms and consisted of (1) difficulty finding information about the 4Ms, (2) poor 4Ms data quality, (3) sparse EHR data sharing, (4) variable intrafacility practices, and (5) homegrown 4Ms EHR tools. Interviewees shared some examples of tools that had been implemented in their practice settings that increased access to 4Ms data, including documentation search workarounds, trackboards, and alerts. Conclusions: Among a sample of clinicians and clinical staff representing large academic medical centers, 4Ms data in the EHR were characterized by multilevel barriers related to access and accuracy. Alternatively, interviewees demonstrated innovative EHR-embedded tools to improve accessibility of some 4Ms-relevant data. These findings inform the future development and refinement of a comprehensive geriatric 4Ms EHR tool for the emergency department and inpatient setting.
title: Aligning the Electronic Health Record With Age-Friendly Care in Hospitals: Qualitative Multisite Study
